item.title: Why a Short Week Can Feel So Long
item.description:
Career

Why a Short Week Can Feel So Long

How changes to a routine can leave leaders exhausted.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Changing direction all day can wear leaders down, even when the individual tasks are manageable.
  • Unfinished work can stay on our minds long after we've moved to the next task.
  • Interruptions may help people finish faster but can also increase stress and effort.
The work may get done, but constantly changing direction can leave a leader exhausted.
Source: Jeff Frey, used with permission

In interviews for my research on leaders, I asked executives to describe a difficult week. One leader talked me through an annual report, tax paperwork, fundraising, board work, and decisions about products and events. When I asked what was hard, she didn't single out any one task, but said, “It's not that those things are too much; it's just the changing of direction every day.”

She could handle the questions, meetings, and requests. What wore her down was having to stop all the normal stuff to deal with the annual report or tax filing, then switch to something else, and then figure out where she'd left off.

I drive my ninth-grade son to school, and yesterday he said it “felt like a long school week.” Interestingly, he had Tuesday off, an early dismissal Wednesday, and a late start Thursday… he actually spent less time at school. So, how could it feel longer!?

It reminded me of the leader story. He and I talked about routines and how little attention we pay to things when we know what comes next. Bottom line… it felt exhausting to have his normal schedule interrupted.

Let's go take a look at what research says about having to change directions so often.

When the Day Won't Hold Still

What did our interrupted leader do? She tried to put some order around the week, setting aside one morning for product development and another stretch of time for board work. Then an event would need attention, or another responsibility would intrude. One day, a staff member left with little notice, and the website, online store, and event preparation were back on her desk. She could plan the week, but keeping it that way was basically impossible.

In 2001, researchers Joshua Rubinstein and his colleagues asked people to switch back and forth between simple tasks, like sorting shapes or doing math. Even small changes took extra time. Harder tasks made it worse, while a clue about what was coming next helped. This wasn't the same as someone interrupting you at work, but it shows that changing gears isn't free. My son knew that his strange school schedule would be back to normal the following week, but the executive had no idea what would interrupt her next.

But the lost time isn't the only issue. I get to interview spouses in my work. The leader mentioned above? Her husband saw what those days did to her. He told me she came home worn out with a long to-do list still on her mind. When she couldn't finish it, he said it “really puts a burden... a strain, on her.” Researcher Sophie Leroy studied something similar in 2009. In two experiments, she found that people had trouble letting go of a task they hadn't finished. Even after moving on to something else, part of their attention was still on the earlier job. She called that “attention residue.”

Think about sitting down to talk with an employee while you're still worrying about the budget you left unfinished.

Here's the most surprising finding to me around this subject: in 2008, Gloria Mark and her colleagues had people do typical office email tasks. Some were interrupted by calls or instant messages. The interrupted people actually finished their work FASTER… and their work wasn't noticeably worse (although their email replies were shorter). So why not be interrupted all day if you’re more productive? Those interrupted workers felt more stressed, frustrated, and rushed, and said the work took more effort.

Prep Before You Switch

The executive's week wasn't hard because of any one task. It was having to stop, switch, and figure out where she'd left off, over and over again. My son's week wasn't harder because of the assignments. It was having to think about what comes next and what comes after and hold that in the front of his mind.

Remember Sophie Leroy's finding about “attention residue”? In 2018, she and Theresa Glomb tested a way to reduce it. In their studies, people took a moment before switching tasks to think about where they'd stopped and how they'd pick up again. They called it a “ready-to-resume” plan. It helped people focus on the new task instead of worrying so much about the unfinished one.

So, here's how to fix a heavy, mixed-up week. You're halfway through a report when the phone rings. Before taking the call, jot down where you stopped and what you'll do next when you return. That's it. Now you can give the caller your attention without trying to remember every detail of the unfinished report.

My son's schedule will be back to normal next week. The executive can't count on that. But when she has to change direction, she can take a moment to write down where she left off. That won't stop the interruptions, but it will keep her from spending so much time trying to get back to work.

To lead sustainably, when you have to stop what you're doing, take a moment to plan how you'll start again.

item.title: Are You Hanging On to a Negative Story That Keeps You Stuck?
item.description:
Happiness

Are You Hanging On to a Negative Story That Keeps You Stuck?

How to stop repeating the patterns that make you unhappy.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • We often form negative narratives about the self that become entrenched.
  • We may not realize that much of identity is a story that is constructed and can be deconstructed.
  • Healing involves acknowledging past experiences but not assuming the future will be the same.
Source: AI Generated Image

This morning I was in the dog park with Bucket, my Cocker Spaniel. Bucket’s favorite thing to do is chase sticks; he’d rather chase sticks than eat, sleep, or do almost anything else. Each stick seems to bring him unabashed and unwavering delight, as is evident in his dog smile. That’s the story I’ve written for him anyway… and I’m “sticking” with it.

During this morning’s “sticking” session, Bucket discovered a gigantic, thick, and heavy, unwieldy branch, which he managed to get between his jaws and then proudly carried around in his mouth, snubbing my attempts to offer him smaller, more navigable options. After some time, I noticed that he was starting to notice the squirrels running up a tree, and then another couple of dogs arrived, and I saw him staring at them seemingly with longing, as if he wanted to say hello and play.

Several times Bucket attempted to approach the dogs or run at the squirrels, but each time he tried, he was stymied by his big stick, which kept getting caught on everything he encountered. So too, the other dogs moved away when they saw the big stick coming. Bucket continued to grip onto it because he didn’t yet realize that he had the power to open his jaws and release it. He didn’t understand, yet, that the choice was his; he was the one grasping the very thing that was causing his limitation.

The Stories We Construct

We sometimes do the same thing as humans: we hold onto our self-constructed stories long after they serve us, and long after they’re true in reality. Bucket eventually dropped his stick, but we humans often don’t, and continue living out a frustrating life, unknowingly depriving ourselves of what we really want—gripping onto and remaining loyal to our story, but not to ourselves. We stick with our stories even when our stories keep us stuck and cause us suffering.

If someone’s narrative, for example, is that they are unlovable, even in the face of someone loving them, they reject that truth, dismiss what’s happening in reality, the love they’re receiving, and continue insisting on their unlovable “me” story—the very story, paradoxically, that makes them suffer. Reality be damned, they are loyal to their story, not the facts, and not even to their own happiness.

We may stick with our story, even a negative story, simply because we don’t realize that it’s a story. We’re not aware of the fact that much of what we call “me” is a story, something we construct, and can in fact deconstruct. But we think our assumptions about ourselves, our “me” story, are fundamental truth—just who we are. The problem is that our “me” story is inside the lens through which we see everything in our life. The “me” whose identity story we’ve created is the one interacting with and experiencing reality, and reporting back to us on it. And what we experience is inherently interpreted and corrupted through the beliefs of this self-made “me” lens. In order to free ourselves and take off our “me” lenses, we need to see the seer, to get behind the lens through which we’re looking. We need to ask ourselves again and again what we believe about ourselves before anything else happens; what we are coming into the situation already assuming. We have to get behind the eyes through which we’re looking at and experiencing our life. When you can look at the looker, and question the story about the “me” you’ve constructed, then things change.

Our stories are often built around wounds that we’ve suffered. If, for example. our self-story is that we have to do everything ourselves, no one can help us, it’s not because it’s fun to believe that or feel that way. At some point, we probably needed help and didn’t receive it. Our early caretakers may have been unable to give us what we needed. Maybe they didn’t care or were limited and unable or unwilling to help us. The point is we felt alone. And so we created this story of being fundamentally un-helpable. If we’re somebody who has to do everything for ourselves, and no one can help; if we can know that for sure. If it’s set in stone, then we don’t have to mourn the fact that we experienced it; it’s just what is—our karma, if you will. Knowing that this is who we are, we feel more in control; we don’t have to hope for help or be sad or angry about the fact that we didn’t receive it. We don’t have to question why this happened to us, or continues to happen now, because we reject and dismiss the help that’s offered and any evidence that we’re not “all alone.” Furthermore, we don’t ever have to grieve how much we wanted and needed help, and suffered without it. We hold onto the past, counter-intuitively, as a way to not have to mourn and accept the past.

With this as our self-story, locked in place, we can know the kinds of things that happen to us. We don’t have to face the uncertainty of each moment, how it will go, and whether or not we will receive what we need. We don’t have to be vulnerable and ask for help when we need it, because we know we’re not going to get it. Even though our story is not what we want, even though it impedes our connection with others and prevents the opportunity to feel gratitude, even though it gets in the way of our satisfaction and happiness, nonetheless, it becomes our identity and a way to protect ourselves, avoid grief, shame, uncertainty, and the hope that things really can change. Our self-story, as awful as it is, becomes a kind of security blanket. We are secure in the knowing that we won’t get what we need.

Freeing Ourselves From the Narrative

The story we’re holding onto about who we are might not be true, that is, if we stopped proving it were true. It might be something we could drop, like Bucket and his stick. But to let it go can feel even more painful than sticking with our negative story. To let it go can feel like we’re abandoning our suffering, moving from it as if it’s no longer part of us. Paradoxically, it feels too painful to move on from our story of pain.

But getting free is not about dropping your story as if that experience never happened. It is about honoring the wound that the story triggers, grieving and acknowledging what you have experienced—but—without the assumption that this present moment is going to be the same, and without the story that this is who you are, a person whose life is always “like this.” The wound matters, the story can be dropped.

Are you carrying a stick that you're ready to drop?

item.title: 10 Subconscious Reasons You Buy Things You Don't Need
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

10 Subconscious Reasons You Buy Things You Don't Need

The psychology and sociology of consuming.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • We were thrown into an economic system that we didn’t choose, yet we can’t imagine any other.
  • Keeping up with the Joneses is both futile and exhausting.
  • Some people play capitalism as if it were a me-against-them game.

Justin Owens offers a brilliant sociological diagnosis that categorizes the propensities of people from different social classes: “Rich people buy time, poor people buy things, and middle class people buy the appearance of being rich, which is why they stay middle class… Performing wealth costs you the real thing while producing only the appearance of it.”

Would you ever admit to performing being wealthier than your bank account affords?

For those of us without infinite income, every purchase costs hours of our precious finite lives. When we shop for something other than essential items, often we’re actually also shopping for belonging, escapism, repairing the past, justifying the present, trying to control the future, rebelling, and for many other reasons not listed on the packaging. The dopamine spike of each purchase is real enough; however, it simply doesn’t address the root causes of our consumption or recognize that each shopping victory has an expiration date that’s probably much sooner than we imagine.

Here are 10 reasons we may buy things we don’t need.

1. Status coding and climbing

Status coding is the everyday practice of sending signals to our fellow tribe members; its anxious version is status climbing, which is when we project a class above the one we were born into in the hope that the higher-status tribe we admire will recognize us as one of their own.

2. Work justification

We reward ourselves for a long and arduous workweek with something that temporarily promises to make the time-sacrifice worthwhile. Then on Monday morning, we’re back on the same hamster-wheel adding value to billionaires’ stock portfolios when Friday night’s Dubai chocolate is long gone.

3. Virtue signaling

We want others to think we’re virtuous sustainability warriors and not just self-indulgent hedonists, so we buy the “right” brand or the carbon offset or donate to charity to signal to our friends that we are really decent humans.

4. Distraction

Babies are easily distracted by shiny objects, and adults can be just like babies with larger wallets.

5. Overcoming childhood scarcity trauma

We grew up “limited” and couldn’t have everything we wanted when we wanted it, so now we feel it symbolizes success to not have to ration and budget like we did when the only money we had was what we earned from our newspaper routes.

6. Magical unrealism

We see a new object and believe it has the magical ability to make us look or feel younger. My body doesn’t naturally produce enough quercetin, NAD, NAC, curcumin, fish oils, or any of the other 10 million supplements that promise to make me look and feel like a teenager again. But do they really work and how much is the placebo effect?

7. Impostor syndrome

We actually suffer from low self-esteem and are wary that other people might find out that we really didn’t sign up for this thing called adulthood with its thousands of responsibilities and constant crisis management, so we pad our grins with the markers of financial happiness and the agreed-upon symbols of putative success so that others can’t see the inner doubt and misery.

8. Capitalist identity

We were thrown into an economic system that we didn’t choose, yet we can’t imagine any other, which is why Burning Man or “all-inclusive” holidays where you don’t need or can’t use money are so psychologically interesting. Go seven days without buying anything if you want some insights into who you really are when you’re not a wallet with legs.

9. Individualism and independence

Purchasing things we don’t need provides the illusion of autonomy and control. We want to feel like the masters of our destinies and clicking on Amazon buttons makes us feel like Captain Kirk commanding the Starship Enterprise.

10. Gamification

In the 1980s, there was a bumper sticker that read, “Whoever dies with the most toys wins.” Some people are playing capitalism as if it were a me-against-them game.

Bonus: A negotiation with mortality

Every day, we grow closer to dying, and yet we don’t want to believe it. Filling our lives up with possessions that require our attention lessens the dreadful time we can spend pondering the nature of our brief existences, how we are interacting with others, and how we are impacting the earth.

Owens’ piercing insights about consumers should help raise consciousness around what we’re really trying to accomplish when we shop and especially when we impulse-buy. Have we been duped into believing magical characteristics of consuming that don’t really exist? Do we believe that each next purchase represents opening a new and potentially happier chapter of our lives?

Keeping up with the Joneses is both futile and exhausting.

A deep breath while watching a magnificent sunset doesn’t require a financial transaction.

We might want to spend less time trying to fill our lacks with consumption and more time filling them with what our souls really crave: loving relationships.

item.title: Love Beyond Words
item.description:
Relationships

Love Beyond Words

Which comes first: love or communication?

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Good communication results from emotional connection, not vice versa.
  • We don’t fight and shut down over poor communication.
  • We fight and shut down to numb the pain of disconnection.

Many popular magazines and websites offer advice on how to improve "communication,” which they claim will improve marriages. Some of those same venues regularly publish diets and weight-loss tips. You probably know the research findings about the latter—they range from unhelpful to harmful. The better weight-loss tips are as informative as the better communication recommendations. Eat less, move more; speak respectfully, listen attentively.

When couples describe the early part of their relationships, they report that they communicated very well. (Not many newlyweds mouth the great marriage lament: "We just can't communicate!") The prevalence of communication tips in the media implies that for many people, something about marriage degrades the neurons responsible for communication skills.

Good Communication Results From Connection, Not Vice Versa

Of course, problems in love relationships do not occur because people are too stupid to figure out common-sense methods of communication or too dispirited by relationship experience to remember how they used to communicate. It’s misleading to say that people in distressed relationships have communication problems at all, though it can feel that way in their frustration and sadness. It’s more helpful to recognize that they have connection problems.

Communication in love relationships is a function of emotional connection. When people feel connected, they communicate fine, and when they feel disconnected, they communicate poorly, regardless of their choice of words and communication techniques.

How Communication Techniques Can Make Things Worse

When people are emotionally disconnected, the use of communication techniques makes them feel manipulated, and not just because the most popular ones are unnatural, more suited for a therapist's office than a living room. There is usually a hidden agenda in the use of communication techniques—to manipulate partners into giving the response we think is right.

Almost all my newly referred couples feature one partner accusing the other of misusing the communication techniques they learned from previous therapists.

"You're purposely not doing it right.”

"Anyone with common sense could get this.”

"I'm validating you more than you're validating me!"

I've often heard people who've been through communication therapy take great care to use "I-statements" when addressing a partner: "I feel blamed right now," which is, of course, blaming the partner for blaming. These are not communication problems. The partners communicate in subtext exactly what they mean: "You’re failing me.”

Why We Fight and Shut Down

People do not fight and stonewall for lack of communication techniques. They fight and shut down because they feel like their partners don't care or aren't interested in how they feel. They fight and shut down to numb the pain of disconnection.

Feelings of connection are rooted in attunement of emotional states. Though it doesn't have to be positive (you can be attuned to your spouse at the funeral of a loved one), attunement cannot exist in a state of emotional reactivity, when a negative feeling in one causes chaos or shutdown in the other. It is extremely difficult to regulate emotional reactivity with words, even when there is no hidden motivation to convey that the other is failing or defective.

Negative reactivity can be regulated into positive attunement only through interest and caring; they have to be interested in and show sympathy for each other. Interest and caring, like all emotional states, are conveyed primarily by facial expressions, body language, and tone of voice, not by words or communication techniques.

Before You Try to Communicate

Don't think of how to get your partner to do what you want—or, if you prefer the euphemism, how to communicate. Rather, ask yourself these questions:

Do you want to feel emotionally connected with your partner?
How curious are you to learn your partner’s perspective?
Do you care how your partner feels right now?
What do you love and value about your partner?

Having answered those questions, decide whether your connection is more important than the topic of your communication. You must convey that you will love and value your partner despite disagreement. Anything short of this devalues the connection—it's less important than what you want to talk about—thereby guaranteeing negative reactivity.

You Know How to Do It

Think of times when you felt emotionally connected to your partner. Communication was not a chore that required techniques, strategies, precise timing, or careful choice of words. You were interested. You put things awkwardly sometimes, but it didn't matter, because you cared.

Emotional connection is a mental state and a choice. Early in your relationship, you chose to feel connected—just as, if you're thinking about communication techniques now, you may be choosing to feel disconnected.

Forget about communication techniques and choose to feel connected right now. If you do, you'll have a reasonable chance of your partner reciprocating. You can then communicate better. More importantly, you will move closer to re-creating a love beyond words.

item.title: What If Talking About Your Anxiety Isn't Helping?
item.description:
Anxiety

What If Talking About Your Anxiety Isn't Helping?

Conversations about our worries can sometimes make us feel worse.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety venting encourages speaking in extremes, which sometimes distorts our thinking.
  • Too much thinking about and talking about worries can detract from productive action.
  • Some simple guidelines can help make conversations about anxiety more productive.

“What’s on your mind today?” “What’s been going on lately?” “What is activated for you today?” “How have you been feeling?"

Conversations about anxiety run in loops.
Source: Liza Summer/Pexels

Over the years, I have cycled through various go-to opening questions in my anxiety therapy sessions. Sometimes I don’t have to say a word: A client pulls open their Notes app or a journal the moment they sit down on the couch.

Yet, even if I ask the perfect question, or my client has already prepared a list of subjects for the session, the truth is: talking about anxiety doesn’t always lead to healing.

Anxiety runs in a loop. By the time the anxious client has entered my office, they have probably gone over these worries many times. Anxiety likes to replay the same line of thinking until it blurs the border between truth and fiction.

Anxiety venting encourages speaking in extremes, which sometimes distorts our thinking. The other person in the conversation may feel the need to validate our emotions and be supportive, but our brains can interpret this social nicety as an agreement with the content of our worries.

When we engage in a monologue about our anxiety, we are effectively overthinking out loud.

Our brain is trying to self-soothe by overthinking. The hope is that thinking will lead to a solution, clarity, or insight, and then we will feel much better. But as we all know, overthinking our worries can be counterproductive at best and dysregulating at worst.

Thinking about and talking about worries can deepen anxiety. When we spiral down into our thoughts, we go deeper into our heads. We can get lost in the effort to figure out our thoughts.

The solution is action

As an anxiety therapist, my job is to break the cycle of overthinking and help my client spiral up into action. Sometimes, this means that we cannot spend our session talking about anxiety. We cannot analyze and replay the anxious line of thinking.

We have to disrupt the pattern.

The remedy for overthinking is an action that takes you out of your head and back into your life. We change our behavior to change our mindset.

For certain people, such action takes the form of ERP (exposure response prevention). In this type of therapy, a person intentionally faces fears and resists compulsions (including overthinking).

Exposure therapy is quite different from traditional talk therapy. In this approach, a person creates and executes a brave to-do list (formally known as an exposure hierarchy). For example, a person worried about speaking up to their boss practices role-playing the conversation and then sends an email to get a meeting on the books. Someone anxious about driving at night practices driving two blocks in their neighborhood at dusk. The aim is to create a pathway toward facing fears rather than thinking and talking about them.

Exposure therapy means committing to action rather than staying stuck in the analysis of anxiety.

Getting a different perspective on our anxiety

This is not to say that talking about one’s anxiety is never helpful. In some cases, the other person in an anxiety conversation is a valuable source of insight.

When anxiety has caused someone to depart significantly from reality, sharing one’s worries can be grounding. The second person might be able to show where the worrier has created anxious distortions—self-blaming, catastrophizing, or personalizing.

Talking about one’s anxiety also helps when someone feels very alone in their worries. Having a person to share with can help the worrier feel supported, even if the other cannot change their mindset.

Talking about anxiety with a professional can help you get a fresh perspective.
Source: Anotni Shikraba/Pexels

Three rules for healthy conversations about anxiety

Conversations about anxiety will happen, inside and outside of the therapy room. Following these guidelines can help make sure the talk is productive.

Rule #1: Notice and limit how often you repeat the same anxious thoughts

Anxious looping is all about repeating the same well-worn thoughts without making progress. Notice and stop yourself if you are doing this out loud. You are perpetuating a cycle.

Rule #2: If you are asking for a different perspective or reassurance, let it sink in

Too often, we seek insight from another person, but then ignore their view. If you are deep in your anxious worry, someone else’s thoughts are likely a helpful anchor to reality. Do not immediately dismiss what you are hearing from your trusted confidante.

Rule #3: Do not let anxious conversation interfere with concrete action

Discussing your anxiety can be productive to a point, but notice if it is interfering with taking real action. Anxiety can be paralyzing. Remember that spiraling up often involves taking one brave step toward a fear.

Be aware of how discussing your anxiety is taking you out of your present moment. Are you less connected to today because you are talking about fears for the future or worries about the past? Conversations can help people cope, but sometimes they pull people deeper into thought.

If you are stuck, take a break from talking about worries. Instead, today, do one small thing for yourself that brings joy.

item.title: Could Upskilling Save Your Marriage?
item.description:
Marriage

Could Upskilling Save Your Marriage?

Couples can work on these relationship skills even before counseling.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • A marriage doesn't fall apart overnight.
  • The slow wear of a marriage running on autopilot can show in small ways.
  • If you no longer share values or one of you doesn't want to be there, there may be a crack in the foundation.

Two weeks before he turned 50, David Levin was in counseling trying to save his marriage. But just a couple of minutes into the second of three sessions they'd agreed to try, his wife said she didn't want to do this anymore and wanted a divorce.

In the years since, he found himself using skills that, he says, arrived one marriage too late. "I had real time to ask who I was and what made me happy. I became a more present father, because my time with the kids suddenly felt finite."

He also noticed his divorced friends felt the same: "That's when it clicked. None of this actually required a divorce. It just required the time and a push."

He's put his experience, research, and insights from his own therapeutic sessions (pre- and post-divorce), into writing his first book: A Divorced Dad’s Playbook for the Still-Married: Hard-won secrets so you can be a better partner, parent & person.

Certified divorce coach Justin Milrad says, "A marriage doesn't fall apart overnight. It's a gradual accumulation of resentment, disconnection, unmet expectations, conversations that could've, should've, or never happened."

Milrad read Levin's book just as he was getting married for the second time: "Even though I've done the work, it reminded me of what I need to do better, what I need to focus on, and how I can show up authentically for myself and for my new wife."

Friction or a Cracked Foundation?

Levin describes friction as the slow wear of a marriage: "A lot of households run on mind-reading. One partner quietly holds the whole family's inventory in their head, and the other has no idea that inventory exists."

On the other hand, Levin cautions, crisis is when the foundation itself is cracked: you no longer share core values, or one of you doesn't want to be there. "Ours was a foundation problem. The marriage had probably ended years before anyone said it out loud."

"A good tell for friction is that you still want to be in the room together, but you mostly talk about logistics," says Levin. "A tell for crisis is that you've stopped talking about the marriage at all."

He believes that most marriages that feel like they're failing don't actually have a cracked foundation; the couple just has skills problems that look like foundation problems. "Your marriage is probably fine. That's not a compliment, and it isn't an insult. It's where most of us live."

"A Divorced Dad's Playbook for the Still-Married" book cover.
Source: David Levin, used with permission

Specific, Learnable Skills

Upskilling in specific areas can strengthen a marriage. Levin speaks from experience when he says that skills can be learned but almost nobody works on them until it’s too late. He outlines 71 skills in his book, but he sees couples struggling the most with these:

Presence. Being in the room for real, not just physically.

Saying the good thing. One specific appreciation, out loud, every day. Most of us save our charm for strangers.

Making the invisible visible. One shared calendar and a 15-minute weekly check-in, so nobody has to read minds.

No tag-outs. Each partner able to run the whole household alone, so neither one becomes the default parent.

Not keeping score. Own your part first, and make a proposal instead of a case.

Courting. Putting yourselves back on the calendar, and treating date night like a date, not a logistics meeting.

Normalizing Therapy

Levin says one of the main reasons he wrote his book was to help normalize therapy for people who've never tried it: "I think therapy is amazing and everyone should be in it."

Much of the experiences Levin includes in his book came out of his own therapy, including Gottman's Four Horsemen and Nonviolent Communication: "The book is one layperson explaining to another what therapy can actually feel like. My therapist, Lauren Demby, LCSW, comes up a lot in the book, and she's a big part of why I'm such a believer."

Milrad agrees: "I never, in a million years, thought I'd be divorced or be a divorce coach, [but] I saw the opportunity to reinvent my life. What I offer is complementary to therapy. It's radical acceptance: tell me about the life you want to live, and then we figure out how to create that life."

"When you're going through a divorce, if you're doing it right, in my opinion," says Milrad, who also hosts The Conscious Divorce Podcast and is the author ofYou 2.0: Divorce, a Better Way Forward and co-author of The Co-Parenting Playbook. "You're working on yourself: about what went well, what could I have done better, if I were to do it again next time, what would I change?"

He says divorce can provide a chance to step off the "hamster wheel of life" and figure out how to create systems that are effective in another relationship.

Divorce Can Also Be a Blessing

Both Milrad and Levin stress that, sometimes, divorce is where you end up. And they want to reduce the stigma that it's somehow a failure or that the relationship was a mistake.

"It's OK to get divorced, and it can be one of the greatest blessings if you can have an amicable relationship with your ex, and if your kids are in a good place, and you find a happier place to be," assures Milrad. "And you should want the same for your ex, as well."

After doing the work to understand himself, Levin says, "I'm happier now than I've been in years."

item.title: How Video Games Make Money by Tracking Your Behavior
item.description:
Career

How Video Games Make Money by Tracking Your Behavior

Do video games and apps use your data to keep you engaged?

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Video games and apps track your behavior while using their apps.
  • Developers use this and other information about you to maximize profits.
  • Some games become easier, harder, or impossible depending on what choices they think you will make.

Many video games cheat. Even games that seem fair on the surface use clever tricks to manipulate you into spending more time and money than you otherwise would.

Researcher Ayo Omolewa decompiled a number of popular games and apps, including Block Blast, Subway Surfers, and Candy Crush, to see how they work. He discovered that many of these games twist and change to maximize the amount of money they think they can make from you. Like a living thing, these apps analyze how you play, how skilled you are, and how much pain you’re willing to put up with and then adjust themselves accordingly.

In January 2026, the game Block Blast by developer Hungry Studio was the most downloaded game in the world. About three hundred million people played it that month.

In Block Blast, players work to drag and drop randomly selected tiles into a grid. When one places a tile in a way that completes a row or column, the row or column is removed, like finishing a row in Tetris, making room for further tiles. The game ends when there is no room to place the remaining tiles.

It is designed to feel like a luck-based strategy game. Which of the three blocks should you place first and where? “If I put this first block into the top corner, it will clear that row, which should give me space to place the second one…”

However, because this is a free-to-play game, the developers need to find ways to make money. I wrote about how free-to-play games make money by manipulating players in more detail here.

In this game, it’s by making you watch ads. In addition to a rotating set of ads below the playable area, whenever players lose, they can either restart the level and lose their progress, or watch an optional advertisement.

Making a game like this would be relatively simple, but based on Omolewa’s research, the developers appear to have added extra code to maximize the chance players would watch ads. Omolewa found that the game tracks more than 250 variables for each player. The game uses this data to determine when you’re most likely to watch an ad and then pounces.

It turns out that the set of tiles the game offers you isn’t random after all.

For example, it keeps track of how many ads you’ve watched in a row. Once you’ve watched three in a row, you’ve demonstrated that you’re willing to sit through advertisements. It then watches your score and waits until you’re at least 10% above your high score. It knows that you’re invested, because you’re doing better than you ever have.

It then waits until an ad is worth at least 3.5 times the money as the last ad you watched. Once you meet these criteria (you’ve watched three ads in a row, you’re doing well, and the next ad will earn the developers enough money), it triggers the “death algorithm.” (“Death algorithm” isn’t a phrase I invented; it’s literally in the game’s code.)

At this point, the game stops offering random sets of tiles and starts looking for a set of tiles that is impossible to place. Every turn from then on, you will have a 20% chance of receiving that set and losing. There’s no way to win with those tiles. If you want to continue, you will have to watch the ad.

Once it’s worth enough to the developers, they force you to lose. No amount of skill or strategy can salvage your game. Only watching an ad can.

Omolewa found several algorithms like this within the game's code. Some keep track of how often you play the game. Others consider what model phone you have, what country you’re playing in, even how you originally came across and downloaded the game. These are all used to calculate how much they will earn from you watching an ad and how likely you are to play tomorrow to determine exactly how much pain they can put you through without becoming so frustrated that you stop playing. You can read his full breakdown here.

In other words, what appears at first to be a simple block placing game is really a money-making machine that tracks your location, phone, and everything you do in the game to make you lose exactly when you’re going to make them as much money as possible.

Although this game seems to use this information only to get users to watch more ads, others track you in similar ways to keep you coming back and spending money. He found in Subway Surfers’ code that the game becomes easier or harder depending on how much money you’ve paid over time, how long it’s been since you’ve watched an ad, and more than 150 other variables.

Candy Crush may similarly adjusts the current difficulty, but also changes the rewards for watching an ad and the prices of in-game bonuses based on how well you’ve been performing, how close you are to beating the current level, how well you’re doing in the weekly rankings, how often you watch the optional ads, and how often you’ve given the app real money. Even the language-learning app Duolingo seems to monitor variables like what kinds of notifications get you to open the app most frequently and tracks what Wi-Fi network you’re on to see if you’re home before pushing a reminder notification.

Games and apps like these leave nothing to chance. They’re constantly tracking and analyzing everything you do: every time you open the app, every click, every payment, your skill level, your willingness to watch ads, and hundreds of other variables to tweak the game to maximize the chance that you’ll watch an ad or give them money. Keep this in mind the next time a game asks you for something. They’ve probably been building a profile on you and using it to their advantage.

Andrew is the author of Parenting a Gamer: Help Your Child Build Healthy Habits, Make Positive Choices, and Find Balance in Virtual Worlds.

item.title: Parenting the Emotionally Intense Child
item.description:
Parenting

Parenting the Emotionally Intense Child

When emotional expression needs understanding and support.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Expressing emotions intensely is a trait of temperament.
  • All emotions are valid, but not all behavioral responses are acceptable.
  • Persistent dysregulation that negatively affects functioning warrants additional evaluation.

Consider the following. Toddlers are playing at a sensory table that is full of rubber ducks, water, and bubbles. A child takes the duck out of two other children’s hands. One child calmly picks up another duck, while the other child falls on the floor and proceeds to have an epic temper tantrum. The first child in this example has low emotional intensity. This child may experience intense emotions, though their reaction suggests otherwise. The second child in this example has a high level of emotional intensity.

An emotionally intense child expresses emotions with greater fervour than other children of a similar age. Emotionally intense children express incredible happiness, profound sadness, fierce frustration, and overwhelming surprise. They squeal with delight over every birthday present. They sob uncontrollably if a toy breaks while they are playing with it. They may hit their head repeatedly if they spill a glass of milk.

Emotional intensity is not inherently a weakness. In fact, the degree of emotional intensity is a trait of temperament. It is innate and ingrained. With the right support, children who have a high level of emotional intensity can learn to understand their emotions, develop emotional self-regulation skills, and know that they don't need to change who they are to be happy and successful.

Temperament and Biology

Research suggests that the aspects of temperament have both genetic and environmental influences.1 Differences in emotional reactivity emerge early in life, and many remain at the same level as children grow and develop. Yet development, experiences, and relationships can influence how children manage their emotions.

Emotionally intense children are often described as dramatic, stubborn, difficult, overly sensitive, or exhausting. But these labels are damaging and overlook an important distinction: The intensity of a child's emotional response is not the same as their ability to manage that emotional experience.

Strengths of emotionally intense children:

  • Passion and enthusiasm
  • Deep investment in relationships
  • Persistence and determination
  • Awareness

Weakness of emotionally intense children:

  • Easily overwhelmed
  • Difficulty in recovering from disappointment
  • Sensitive to rejection
  • Difficulty managing distress

How to successfully parent an emotionally intense child:

  • Stay calm before you react.
  • Validate the child’s emotion without accepting every behavior.
  • Educate your child when the behavioral response to their emotion was undesired.
  • Provide a consequence for misbehavior if indicated.
  • Explain to your child how they can behave more appropriately in the future.

For example, tell your child, "I understand that you are mad. It's okay to be angry, but it is not okay to hit your brother. Next time, come ask me for help.”

It is important to teach coping skills when the child is calm. Practice labeling emotions, asking for help, problem-solving, and managing frustration during times devoid of conflict or challenges. Yet at the same time, do not automatically rescue children from every disappointment or challenging experience. Provide appropriate support and empower them to navigate challenges. The goal is to help them to trust and believe that "I can experience difficult emotions and still be okay."

Celebrating Emotions

Children benefit from knowing their emotional experiences aren't something to be ashamed of. In fact, children need to understand that their emotions are important, valid, and something to be acknowledged. No emotion is inherently good or bad. No emotion is inherently positive or negative. Emotions are simply experiences created in our own psyche. It is important to allow children to experience their emotions fully, without guilt or shame. Yet at the same time, emotionally intense children need to learn, over time, how to express their emotions in a socially appropriate manner.

When is emotional intensity a sign of something more?

Although emotional intensity can reflect normal temperament, persistent struggles with emotional regulation that negatively affect everyday functioning can also occur with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorders, disruptive mood dysregulation disorder, autism spectrum disorder, depressive disorders, and trauma-related conditions.

When emotional reactions are persistently severe, frequent and/or intense, interfere with school performance, raise concerns about safety, represent significant change from the child's usual behavior, or negatively affect friendships, it is important to reach out to your child’s pediatrician.

Final Thoughts

Emotionally intense children can be explosive. They express their emotions in a dramatic fashion and often possess limited ability to self-regulate. It is important to understand such children. We need to demonstrate patience and compassion. Remember that experiencing emotional intensity is not a choice. Yet emotionally intense children can learn to experience their emotions and express them in an appropriate manner.

item.title: Co-Regulation: We Don’t Outgrow the Rhyme and the Rhythm
item.description:
Career

Co-Regulation: We Don’t Outgrow the Rhyme and the Rhythm

What babies, poets, and sailors can teach us about the nervous system at work.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Humans first learn co-regulation through rhythm, rhyme, and a caregiver’s voice.
  • Rhythm, including shared rhythm, keeps steadying us as adults, through poetry, chant, prayer, and work songs.
  • Neurodivergent stimming is often pathologized, but it uses the same regulation mechanisms.
Man Reading
Source: Hani Hamza / Studio UK

Somewhere right now, a parent is humming the same four notes over and over. The baby in their arms doesn’t understand the words of the song, and there is no need. The rhythm is the message: you are held, you are safe.

Psychologists call this co-regulation, one nervous system lending calm or strength to another. Some of the earliest communication occurs through rhythm.

The first language is a heartbeat

The research reveals the power of early, embodied communication. When mothers and infants interact face to face, their heart rhythms begin to coordinate (Feldman et al., 2011). Infants stay calm about twice as long when sung to as when spoken to, even when the song is in a language they’ve never heard (Corbeil et al., 2016). In one study, infants relaxed to lullabies from distant cultures; their heart rates slowed, and their pupils narrowed to songs whose words they could not possibly recognize (Bainbridge et al., 2021).

Something in the sweet repetition of a lullaby speaks directly to the body. Nursery rhymes do the same, while also teaching language.

But embodied communication is not just for babies. We don’t outgrow the rhyme and the rhythm. We don't outgrow the need for deep connection. We just give them grown-up names: poetry, song, prayer.

What adults call deep communication

We call it poetry. Something in metered verse reaches the body before the mind catches up. We listen to poetry and get goosebumps. It activates the brain’s reward regions (Wassiliwizky et al., 2017). In an experiment, when people recited verse in a steady meter (hexameter verse used by Homer in the Iliad and Odyssey), their heart rate began to synchronize with the rhythm of their breath — more so than with breathing exercises (Cysarz et al., 2004). The ancient bards reciting epics by the fire weren’t just telling stories. They were tuning up the listeners’ bodies. Poetry is co-regulation.

We call it song. Strangers who sing together bond faster (Pearce et al., 2015), and when choir members sing in unison, their heart rates synchronize (Vickhoff et al., 2013). Some songs unite entire nations. In 1792, an officer wrote a marching song for French troops near the Rhine. As it spread, volunteers from Marseille sang it, and the city’s name became associated with it. The Marseillaise turned crowds of strangers into a people who breathed as one. It has been sung ever since in moments of defiance, wherever people needed to borrow courage from each other and from prior generations.

We call it a work song. For centuries, sailors tied their knots to shanties, field workers kept pace with call-and-response, and laborers raised walls to a shared beat. The songs coordinated muscle movements while also carrying humor, hope, grief, and protest. They made hard work more bearable by stressing the human connection.

And we call it prayer. Reciting rhythmic prayers regulates breathing and the heart’s rhythms (Bernardi et al., 2001). But the type of prayer seems to matter: God-focused prayers such as gratitude and adoration are linked to greater well-being than more obligatory or self-focused forms (Whittington & Scher, 2010).

Does your workplace need a lullaby?

Emotions are contagious. One irritated person can shift the mood of a whole team, and that mood shapes cooperation and conflict (Barsade, 2002). Dysregulation threatens the quality of decision-making, performance, and talent retention.

Yet most workplaces treat regulation as an individual’s job, to be handled silently, with sheer willpower and perhaps an app. But humans have always steadied each other.

Rituals help reduce anxiety (Hobson et al., 2016), strengthen coworker bonds, and increase helping (Yim et al., 2025). A team doesn’t need a nursery rhyme or a sea shanty, but a poem, a meaningful ritual, or sharing in authentic gratitude can help a group of adults find common ground and a source of calm.

Neurodivergent rhythms and regulation we judge

Many autistic adults describe using stimming, rhythmic movement, or vocalization to help self-regulate and cope with the unfriendly world (Kapp et al., 2019). These behaviors are often treated as symptoms to be extinguished or are stigmatized as "unprofessional." Yet they use the same neural self-regulation mechanism as the ancient work song, the chant, and the lullaby.

When neurotypical people regulate through rhythm, it is called tradition, worship, or team spirit. When neurodivergent people do it, it is often called a problem. A neuroinclusive culture recognizes the tool as universal and lets people use it in their own way. And perhaps learn from their deeper connection to timeless human wisdom that modern societies too often pretend to have outgrown. Neurodivergent people might, once again, offer a canary-in-the-coal-mine insight into something that benefits everyone.

Tools are neutral; uses are not

Rhythm is powerful, and power can be misused. La Marseillaise calls for an enemy’s “impure blood” to water the fields. The same rhythm that binds a people together can also bind them against someone. Rituals forced on people become a source of stress rather than comfort. Co-regulation is helpful when it is offered, not imposed or manipulative (Yim et al., 2025).

A parent humming a lullaby doesn’t demand that the baby calm down or attempt to squeeze performance. A bard by the fire shares wisdom without imposing one's own will. Workplaces could learn from that: care works better than coercion, and companionship works better than control.

This post is an expanded version of my presentation: Praslova, L. (2026, November 12). Poetry, neuroinclusive connection, and the ethical organization [Conference keynote]. Poetry in Business, Nov. 12-13, Virtual.

item.title: The Most Important Sign You're in the Wrong Relationship
item.description:
Friends

The Most Important Sign You're in the Wrong Relationship

Detecting emotional danger through how you feel.

Posted November 15, 2026

Key points
  • Pay attention to how you feel with your partner: comfortable and content, or nervous and unsettled.
  • Beware of attempts to isolate through prioritizing private time alone together.
  • Mismatched relational investment is a sign your prospective paramour is moving faster than you are.

Your new paramour seems too good to be true. Attentive and thoughtful, he or she says all of the right things and anticipates your needs and desires before you do. Yet as time goes on, you feel unsettled and insecure when you are together, and even when you are apart—due to your partner's demand for constant communication. You begin to desire time to yourself, even though you are just getting to know your new love interest. Have you suddenly become more independent, or is there something else going on?

Source: StockSnap / Pixabay

The Gift of Instinct

The most important indication you are in the wrong relationship is not necessarily what your friends think about your paramour, or his or her public persona; it is how your partner makes you feel. Fortunately, we are all gifted with the intuition to detect potential discomfort or even danger when spending time with other people, especially one-on-one.

Dark Personalities Impact Partner Mental Health

Shahida Arabi (2023)[i] investigated the impact of partner narcissism and psychopathy on partner post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), noting that dark personalities may shower romantic prospects with excessive attention and flattery commonly referred to as “love bombing,” as a tactic of manipulation, particularly at the beginning of a relationship. Yet she also notes that dark personalities shut down conversations or "stonewall," and even “gaslight” partners by questioning their memory, reality, or perception. Arabi explains that one narcissism subtype, grandiose narcissism, is linked with high amounts of self-esteem and self-confidence, which, as a practical matter, could cause a partner on the receiving end of such negative behavior to second-guess their perception and self-worth.

Fortunately, regardless of partner personality type, there are ways to recognize your discomfort before remaining in the wrong relationship. Here are a few clues.

  1. Constant contact. Although we all enjoy attention, there can be too much of a good thing. Texting multiple times a day makes us uncomfortable, even apprehensive of what we perceive to be an overabundance of premature attention. This often includes impatience at a delayed reply.
  2. Time demands. Beware of an expressed desire to see you more than your work or family schedule permits, or more than you are comfortable with.
  3. Inappropriate gifts. Expensive or lavish gifts that are disproportionate to your relational stage are cause for concern. Your partner’s financial display of affection may be designed to create a sense of indebtedness to make you feel as if you owe him or her something in return.
  4. Attempts at isolation. A partner’s attempts to isolate you from your support system are insidious and subtle. Indirect expressions of negativity toward your family, friends, or co-workers designed to discourage you from future contact—especially when the time block conflicts with time your partner desires to spend with you. On holidays and birthdays, you can always include your new paramour; the danger comes when he or she wants you to exclude friends and family.
  5. Mismatched Intentions. In combination, many early warning signs point towards another common denominator that signals relational imbalance: mismatched intensity. Your immediate goal may be companionship, not commitment. A friendship-first approach allows couples to build chemistry, comfort, and trust.

If you feel uncomfortable and unsettled, it is better to pull back sooner rather than later, because mismatched affection tends to get worse, not better. Just like the dashboard warning indicators in your car are yellow before they turn red, a relational partner who green-lights your feelings regarding the progress and pace of your relationship will allow you to safely journey into a quality relationship.
